paragraphs.heading: What mitosis is
paragraphs.text: Mitosis is the step in a cell's life cycle where copied chromosomes are split between two new nuclei. Mitosis is an equational division: the two nuclei it makes are genetically identical, and the chromosome count stays the same. Together, its stages make up the M phase of the cell cycle.

paragraphs.heading: Why it matters
paragraphs.text: Mitosis is how a cell hands its full genome, the set of its chromosomes, to two daughter cells. Chromosomes are tightly coiled bundles of DNA that carry the information a cell needs to work properly. Because every daughter gets the same set, genetic stability is kept across generations of cells. Most human cells come from mitotic division; the big exceptions are sperm and eggs, which are made by meiosis. Bacteria and archaea split by a different process called binary fission.

paragraphs.heading: Getting ready
paragraphs.text: Before mitosis starts, the cell must copy every chromosome. This happens during the S phase of interphase, which comes before mitosis. Each copied chromosome becomes a pair of identical sister chromatids, held together at a point called the centromere by proteins named cohesins.

paragraphs.heading: How it unfolds
paragraphs.text: When mitosis begins, the chromosomes condense and become visible. In some organisms, such as animals, the nuclear envelope, the wrapping that keeps DNA apart from the cytoplasm, breaks up into small vesicles, and the nucleolus, which builds ribosomes, vanishes. Microtubules reach out from opposite ends of the cell, hook onto the centromeres and line the chromosomes up across the middle. Then they contract and pull the sister chromatids apart, and each one is now called a daughter chromosome. As the cell stretches, the daughter chromosomes are dragged to opposite ends.

paragraphs.heading: Stages and finishing
paragraphs.text: Biologists divide the process into stages, each marking the end of one set of tasks and the start of the next. They are preprophase, found only in plant cells, then prophase, prometaphase, metaphase, anaphase and telophase. Afterwards, cytokinesis splits the cytoplasm, organelles and cell membrane, giving two new cells with roughly equal shares.

paragraphs.heading: Not the same everywhere
paragraphs.text: Mitosis varies from one kind of organism to another. Animal cells usually go through open mitosis, in which the nuclear envelope breaks down before the chromosomes separate. Fungal cells usually go through closed mitosis, dividing their chromosomes inside a nucleus that stays whole. Most animal cells also round up into a near-sphere as mitosis starts.

paragraphs.heading: When it goes wrong
paragraphs.text: A faulty division can make three daughter cells, called tripolar mitosis, or more than three, called multipolar mitosis, instead of two. Errors like these can produce embryos that cannot survive and fail to implant. Other errors can trigger mitotic catastrophe, apoptosis (programmed cell death) or mutations, and some cancers can grow out of such mutations.

paragraphs.heading: How it was named
paragraphs.text: In animal cells, mitosis was found in 1873 in cornea cells of frogs, rabbits and cats, and the Polish histologist Wacław Mayzel first described it in 1875. Walther Flemming coined the word in 1882, from the Greek mitos, meaning warp thread. Other names exist too, such as karyokinesis, which means nuclear division.
